newsitem.title: USA: Former Donnelley head to face similar challenges at AT&T.
newsitem.headline: Former Donnelley head to face similar challenges at AT&T.

text.p: John Walter, who transformed R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. from a staid old-line printer to a technology-driven information giant, is likely to face similar challenges at AT&T Corp.

The 49-year-old Walter will leave Donnelley, where he was chairman and chief executive officer, to join AT&T, where he will become president and chief operating officer on Nov. 1, before taking over from AT&T Chief Executive and Chairman Robert Allen in 1998.

Under Walter's direction, Chicago-based Donnelley has beefed up its printing operations in the United States and high-technology information businesses here and abroad. Acquisitions and capital spending have totalled $2 billion in the past five years.
Industry analysts and consultants said that Walter was well-respected for his strategic vision but has never faced a challenge such as the one that looms at AT&T.

"AT&T is the biggest battleship you have ever seen. Donnelly is not a small company, but AT&T is 10 times the revenues and has three times the employees," said Dave Goodtree, a consultant at Forrester Research.
What's more, AT&T sits in the middle of the rapidly changing communications and information industries.
AT&T's Allen, noting how Walter has changed Donnelley into a tough global competitor, said in a statement: "Meeting those challenges is what leading the new AT&T is all about."

"Walter had a clear vision of the big picture where the (printing) industry was going," said Rudolf Hokanson of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "The old Donnelley was slow to change, arrogant and in control -- a quality company but in an old model. Walter changed that."
"He tried to make people more accountable, tried to flatten some of the reporting structure," he said.

Walter also recognised the need for his company to refocus on squeezing the most value from its assets, Hokanson said. He cited the spin-off earlier this year of direct mailer Metromail Corp. and the planned spin-off of Donnelley Enterprise Solutions Inc., a provider of information management services to large law firms and investment banks.
Colleagues have described Walter as "a nonstop worker, intensely focused with a remarkable ability to think ahead and get to the heart of critical issues."

Among Walter's favourite quotes, said Steven Bono, Donnelley's senior vice president for corporate affairs, is: "When you hire, hire people better than you and then you'll build a company of giants. Hire people worse than you and you'll disappear."

AT&T is not the giant it used to be. Its share of the $75 billion long-distance telephone market has fallen to around 55 percent from 60 percent two years ago, with marketing stumbles hitting earnings in the recent third quarter.

Adjusted for the split-off of Lucent Technologies Inc. earlier this year, AT&T's stock has fallen 16 percent in 1996, about the same as the broader market has risen, and its shareholders are restless.
"This is not a candidate to lead the rally," said Barry Sine of SBC Warburg.
But Cable & Wireless Plc Chief Executive Richard Brown noted that Donnelly was a formidable user of technology and has used telecommunications -- including AT&T's -- to transform its business.
"I think AT&T is fortunate to get John Walter. John Walter is a leader ... He know the telecoms world but he is not directly involved. He's a quick study," Brown told Reuters.

Donnelley Chief Financial Officer Cheryl Francis, who is serving on the management committee to find a permanent successor to Walter, said he will leave a legacy of "well-defined principles" for improving the company.

Like Allen at AT&T, Walter worked himself up through the ranks at Donnelley. He earned a bachelor's degree from Miami University in 1969 and joined Donnelley as a sales trainee. He worked in various positions, advancing to president in 1987, and chairman, president and chief executive in 1989.
The soft-spoken Walter, an avid golfer, is married and has two daughters.

Donnelley, whose roots go back to 1864, is the largest supplier of commercial printing and related services in the United States. The company prints magazines, including Time, Newsweek, TV Guide, Reader's Digest and Business Week, among others, encyclopaedias and yellow pages for 35 telephone directory publishers worldwide.
